|Commodity Markets Strategy Group1|16 September 2011| |---|---| |**Metals Market Comment**|| # **Beyond the US Dollar price of gold** ### - **Isolating the USD effect** The 10-year bull market in the gold price has been driven by a number of factors, including inflation concerns and loose monetary conditions, as well as economic and financial uncertainty. Crucially too, as gold is quoted in USD, the depreciation of the currency against other major currencies has played an important role in taking gold higher. In this short note, we attempt to isolate the impact of the USD depreciation on the gold price from other factors. In so doing, we construct indices to reflect an international price of gold weighted by producer and consumer currencies and by share of world GDP. Our indices do not purport to be exhaustive as they do not include 100% of production, consumption or GDP. They are constructed by using the prices in individual currencies multiplied by country weights. Some currencies depreciated inordinately relative to the USD during the observed period. So we have made two indices, one including all currencies, and the other excluding currencies that lost more than 50% of their value between the start of 2001 and the end of 2010. ### - **International gold price indices** In the first instance, we look at the producer gold price. The index, which includes all the top producers, has outperformed the gold price in USD terms. But amongst the top producers, some have seen their currency depreciate sharply over the past 10 years. This is notably the case with Argentina, Venezuela, Guinea, Ghana, Tanzania and Uzbekistan, which accounted for 13% of global production in 2010. Chart 2 compares the USD gold price with a consumer gold price index. The consumer gold price index is calculated using 95% of total physical consumption. Another sub-index has been made excluding Turkey and Iran (4% of our selection) as their currencies depreciated by more than 50% during our observation period. In Chart 3, we show the gold price in USD terms vs. a gold price index using GDP weightings representing 85% of world GDP in 2010, and a sub-index which excludes Venezuela, Argentina and Turkey (3% of selection). ### - **USD effect relatively modest** Looking at the performance of the three sub-indices which exclude outliers, they have all underperformed the USD gold price by about 15%. **Chart 1: Producer gold index** Producer
